content: An academic degree represents a formal recognition of achievement, typically awarded by institutions of higher education such as universities. This recognition is granted upon the successful completion of a structured program of study. Historically, teaching at universities was reserved for individuals who were appropriately qualified. Similar to how a carpenter would progress through the ranks of apprentice and journeyman to become a master carpenter upon certification by their guild, a teacher would attain the title of master after being licensed by their professional teaching guild. These teaching guilds, which operated in various cities, evolved into what we now recognize as universities. This transformation occurred when they were granted charters, often by the Pope or the Holy Roman Emperor in Europe. Students were admitted to these universities and advanced through their academic ranks in a manner analogous to the progression within trade guilds. While institutions of higher education have existed since ancient times, such as Taxila and Nalanda in ancient India, the first institutions to confer academic degrees at all levels (bachelor, master, and doctorate) were the medieval Madrasahs established in the 9th century. The University of Al Quaraouiyine in Fez, Morocco, is recognized by the Guinness Book of World Records as the oldest degree-granting university in the world. It was founded in 859 by Princess Fatima al-Fihri. In the 9th century, Bimaristan medical schools emerged in the medieval Islamic world. These institutions issued medical degrees and diplomas to students of Islamic medicine who were qualified to practice as Doctors of Medicine. The origins of the doctorate can be traced back to the ijazat attadris wa 'l-ifttd (translated as license to teach and issue legal opinions) in the medieval Islamic legal education system. This qualification, equivalent to the Doctor of Laws, was developed during the 9th century following the establishment of the Madh'hab legal schools. To earn a doctorate, students were required to study in a guild school of law, typically for four years at the undergraduate level and at least ten years for postgraduate studies. The doctorate was awarded after an oral examination that assessed the originality of the candidate's thesis and their ability to defend it against objections in scholarly disputations. These disputations were a regular part of the student's academic training. Upon completing their postgraduate education, students were awarded doctorates, granting them titles such as faqih (master of law), mufti (professor of legal opinions), and mudarris (teacher). These titles were later translated into Latin as magister, professor, and doctor, respectively. In medieval European universities, students who completed three or four years of study in the prescribed texts of the trivium (grammar, rhetoric, and logic) and the quadrivium (mathematics, geometry, astronomy, and music)—collectively known as the Liberal Arts—were awarded the degree of Bachelor of Arts. This term, derived from the Latin baccalaureus, was previously used to describe a squire or apprentice to a knight. Further study, particularly successful participation in and moderation of disputations, led to the Master of Arts degree. This degree, derived from the Latin magister (teacher), entitled the holder to teach these subjects. Masters of Arts were eligible to pursue advanced studies in the higher faculties of Law, Medicine, or Theology, earning bachelor's and then master's or doctoral degrees in these disciplines. Thus, a degree was merely a step toward becoming a fully qualified master, which is reflected in the English term graduate, derived from the Latin gradus (step). Today, the terms master, doctor, and professor signify different levels of academic achievement. However, in the medieval university, these terms were equivalent, with their usage in degree names varying by university custom. Most universities conferred the Master of Arts degree, but the highest degree was sometimes termed Master of Theology/Divinity or Doctor of Theology/Divinity, depending on the institution. The earliest doctoral degrees—Doctor of Divinity (D.D.), Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.), and Doctor of Medicine (M.D.)—reflect the historical division of university study into these three fields. Over time, the Ph.D. has become less common in theology and medicine, while studies outside these fields, previously termed philosophy, have expanded into sciences and humanities. This usage persists in the degree of Doctor of Philosophy. The University of Bologna in Italy, regarded as the oldest university in Europe, was the first to confer the degree of Doctor in Civil Law in the late 12th century. It also awarded similar degrees in other subjects, including medicine. The University of Paris used the term master for its graduates, a practice adopted by English universities such as Oxford and Cambridge, as well as the ancient Scottish universities of St. Andrews, Glasgow, Aberdeen, and Edinburgh. The naming of degrees eventually became associated with the subjects studied. Scholars in the faculties of arts or grammar were known as masters, while those in theology, medicine, and law were known as doctors. As study in the arts or grammar was a prerequisite for advanced subjects, the degree of doctor assumed a higher status than the master's degree. This hierarchy led to the modern system, where the Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.), developed in 18thand 19th-century German universities, is a more advanced degree than the Master of Arts (M.A.). The practice of using doctor for all advanced degrees originated in German universities and spread globally. In France, the terminology remains closely tied to the original meanings of the terms. The baccalauréat (comparable to bachelor) is awarded to students who complete secondary education and qualifies them for university admission. Upon university graduation, students receive a licence, qualifying them to teach in secondary schools or pursue higher-level studies. In the past, degrees were sometimes issued directly by monarchs or bishops rather than educational institutions. This practice has largely disappeared, though in Britain, Lambeth Degrees are still awarded by the Archbishop of Canterbury. Only the universities of Oxford and Cambridge permit the Ph.D. (Oxford) or D.Phil. (Cambridge) to be conferred by an individual faculty member.
